item.title: Photos show elaborate preparations for Thailand’s Royal Barges Procession
item.description:
Photos show elaborate preparations for Thailand’s Royal Barges Procession BySAKCHAI LALIT Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 8:44 PM
Share
BANGKOK -- More than 2,000 oarsmen have spent months preparing for a centuries-old Thai royal tradition that will fill Bangkok’s Chao Phraya River with a fleet of intricately decorated barges on Friday.
The Royal Barge Procession is held in time for the annual Buddhist Kathin ceremony, which takes place after the end of Buddhist Lent. Buddhists offer kathin robes to monks who have remained in their monasteries throughout the three-month retreat in the rainy season.
The fleet, consisting of a total of 52 barges, will take King Maha Vajiralongkorn, Queen Suthida and members of the royal family to the Wat Arun Ratchawararam temple.
The 2,200 oarsmen from the Royal Thai Navy started their training in June, learning how to row the barges in unison at a navy dockyard before rehearsing in the river in late July.
The full dress rehearsals were performed twice in late October, drawing spectators along both sides of the river.
The rowers must master not only the precise movements required to maintain the fleet formation of five columns and three lines, but also the traditional boat songs performed during the procession. The songs help coordinate the rowing while portraying Thailand’s cultural tradition.
Thailand's Fine Arts Department has been restoring the wooden barges while preserving their traditional artistic details. The vessels have also undergone safety inspections and decorative work in preparation for the event.

item.title: United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
item.description:
United Arab Emirates says military solutions offer no quick off-ramps to crisis with Iran
The United Arab Emirates hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations to prevent a new confrontation between the U.S. and IranBySARAH EL DEEB Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:43 PM
MANAMA, Bahrain -- The United Arab Emirates’ presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible to avert a new round of confrontation between the U.S. and Iran.
The Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 with joint strikes by the U.S. and Israel followed by attacks by Iran on the Gulf nations, has made it “a watershed year” for the region and the world, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said at a security forum in Bahrain.
“We don’t really want to see another round of confrontation in the region,” Gargash told the audience at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS, that brings together regional and international state, defense and foreign-affairs officials and experts.
Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. He said that no direct talks are being held with the U.S. and that the final outcome depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions.”
In an interview shared on his Telegram channel, Araghchi said Iran hoped that the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.” He said Iran was ready for both defense and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality.”
A possible escalation cast a long shadow over the three-day security forum in Bahrain's capital, Manama.
Gargash, the UAE adviser, said that the current crisis requires “a lot of wisdom, with political tools being our main tools, and the understanding that military solutions will only complicate the current very comp...

item.title: UN’s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years following US-Russia standoff
item.description:
UN’s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years following US-Russia standoff
The U.N.'s peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after 35 years due to a U.S.-Russia standoffByAKRAM OUBACHIR Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:34 PM
CASABLANCA, Morocco -- The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory’s future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa’s northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
“This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period,” Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. “A smaller team reporting to the United Nations’ Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.
Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force’s mandate.
Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an “instrument to internationalize the dispute.''

item.title: Thousands of volunteers build 108 stupas in a day in Bhutan's Gelephu Mindfulness City
item.description:
Thousands of volunteers build 108 stupas in a day in Bhutan's Gelephu Mindfulness City
Buddhist masters have gathered in Gelephu, Bhutan, to witness the construction of 108 stupas in a single dayByANUPAM NATH Associated Press and DEEPA BHARATH Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 1:27 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
GELEPHU, Bhutan -- Buddhist masters from various schools and denominations and about 200,000 people from around the world congregated in Gelephu, Bhutan, on Sunday to witness volunteers erect 108 stupas in a single day.
The newly erected sacred structures, representing Buddha’s enlightenment, anchor Gelephu Mindfulness City. Conceived by Bhutan’s King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck and designed by Danish architects, the city is taking shape as a vibrant economic hub that puts the ideals of ecological sustainability and the happiness of the country's citizens over commercial profit.
The city, currently a small town with a population of about 10,000, is in southern Bhutan along the border with India, about 150 miles (240 kilometers) south of Thimphu, the nation's capital.
Amid massive economic challenges — from rising unemployment and falling birth rates to the mass migration of skilled workers — Bhutanese are pinning their hopes on this city to boost their economy and provide the opportunities that would encourage young people to stay in the country.
Bhutan’s Project 108 is an initiative to install 108 stupas with each standing about 50 feet (15 meters) tall, spaced about 354 feet (108 meters) apart, in a single file along the Mao Chhu river, to appear like a “procession” of monuments, according to the project's website. The number 108 is sacred in Buddhism, which is widely practiced in Bhutan.
These stupas are known as Jangchub Chortens in Vajrayana Buddhism, a major branch that emerged in India around the 5th and 7th centuries B.C. It aims to help practitioners attain enlightenment within a single lifetime.

item.title: Canada's Carney reports progress in trade talks with US. Trump talks up 'concept' of a deal
item.description:
Canada's Carney reports progress in trade talks with US. Trump talks up 'concept' of a deal
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he had a constructive conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump about a potential trade dealByROB GILLIES Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 12:00 PM
TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday he had a constructive conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump about a potential trade deal, with negotiators set to work toward an agreement in the coming weeks as the countries seek to resolve their bitter trade dispute just days before the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump subsequently said both sides had “the concept" of a mutually beneficial deal.
Carney said the conversation built on recent discussions about the outlines of a deal that would create jobs, lower costs for families and protect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.
“Our teams will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Carney wrote on social media.
Hours later, after landing in Iowa for a rally, Trump said, “We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada.”
“We’ve been losing money for many years with Canada, many many years,” he said. “So we have — we are now very close to having a deal.”
The U.S. president mentioned speaking with Carney on Saturday and said the possible agreement is “going to be great for our farmers, great for our country, and it’ll be fine for Canada.”
Trump said the negotiations involved construction of the Keystone XL pipeline and prospects that the agreement could erase tariffs paid by U.S. farmers for Canadian products.
“Part of the agreement is that our farmers will have to pay no tariffs,” he said, even though his comments also made clear that final details had not yet been established.

item.title: The UK's stance on its role in the slave trade is shifting, but reparations remain off the table
item.description:
The UK's stance on its role in the slave trade is shifting, but reparations remain off the table
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has expressed openness to formally apologizing for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave tradeBySYLVIA HUI Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 10:50 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
LONDON -- Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to making a formal apology for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, a significant shift in the U.K.'s position in a long-running debate on whether — and how — the country should right the wrongs of its past.
Ahead of his meeting with Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean this week, Burnham said it is the “right thing to do” to have an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery instead of “sticking our heads in the sand.”
While he rejected calls for the U.K. to pay reparations, Burnham proposed leading a program of debt restructuring to help the poorest countries in the Commonwealth, an association of 56 independent nations that grew out of the British Empire.
His stance received a cautious welcome, but the thorny issue of repayments remains unresolved.
“An apology is an essential first step," a trade bloc of Caribbean countries known as Caricom said in a statement Saturday in response to Burnham's comments. “But an apology without repair is incomplete.”
The Netherlands in 2022 apologized for its role in the slave trade, but no country has paid financial reparations to nations affected by slavery or enslaved people and their descendants.
The U.K. has never formally apologized for its role in the trade, though some British institutions including the Church of England have started to own up to the parts they played.

item.title: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
item.description:
Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region are preparing for the end of a localized ceasefireByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated Press and VOLODYMYR YURCHUK Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 9:06 AM
KHERSON, Ukraine -- Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago.
The White House said that U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce, which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday.
“The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.”
An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers weren't released after the evacuation.
At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy.
But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter.

item.title: Taiwan accuses China of harassment after standoff between coast guard ships
item.description:
Taiwan accuses China of harassment after standoff between coast guard ships
Taiwan’s coast guard has accused China of harassment after a Chinese vessel entered restricted waters near a disputed islandByThe Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 8:11 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan’s coast guard accused China of harassment after a Chinese vessel entered restricted waters near a disputed coral island administered by Taiwan in the South China Sea.
China claims democratically ruled Taiwan as its own breakaway province and has not ruled out the use of force to annex it. Beijing sends warships and military jets near the island almost daily, and in recent months has stepped up coast guard patrols, especially in waters east of Taiwan, raising alarm in Taipei.
The Chinese coast guard vessel entered waters near the Pratas Islands, southwest of Taiwan’s main island, early on Saturday, Taiwan’s coast guard said. It added that a Taiwanese coast guard vessel confronted the Chinese ship and asked it to leave.
At the height of the standoff, the two ships came within just 1 nautical mile (1.9 kilometers) of each other, Taiwan’s coast guard said.
Beijing says the waters it patrols fall under its jurisdiction.

item.title: Serbia marks the second anniversary of a train station tragedy that fueled student protests
item.description:
Serbia marks the second anniversary of a train station tragedy that fueled student protests
Thousands of students and supporters in Serbia have marked two years since a deadly train station disasterByMARKO DROBNJAKOVIC Associated Press and JOVANA GEC Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 7:44 AM
NOVI SAD, Serbia -- A week after a student movement toppled Serbia's strongman Aleksandar Vucic in an election, thousands of students and their supporters on Sunday marked two years since a deadly train station disaster that gave birth to their anti-corruption campaign.
The demand for accountability over the Nov. 1, 2024 collapse of a concrete canopy at the station in the northern city of Novi Sad that killed 16 people launched two years of student-led protests that eventually brought about the stunning defeat of Vucic’s right-wing government at last week's parliamentary elections.
In steady rain and silence, thousands marched in Novi Sad on Sunday in a gesture of respect for the victims. Unlike a year ago, when huge crowds gathered for the first anniversary of the tragedy, participants this year said they now have hope that those responsible for the disaster will be punished.
The students brought 16 wreaths and 16 red hearts — one for each victim — outside the station building. The inscribed names of the victims included children. People cried as they laid down flowers and lit candles. A moment of silence was held.
Many in Serbia believe that the concrete canopy crashed because of flawed renovation work caused by corruption and negligence that prevailed in major state infrastructure projects championed by Vucic's government.
The station renovation was part of a bigger railway reconstruction project with China and neighboring Hungary. Vucic and his ally, former right-wing Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban together toured the renewed Novi Sad station back in 2022.

item.title: Somali pirates seize Iranian fishing vessel, raising fears of attacks on cargo ships
item.description:
Somali pirates seize Iranian fishing vessel, raising fears of attacks on cargo ships
Pirates could use the boat as a “mother ship” for attacks on commercial vessels.ByOMAR FARUK Associated PressNovember 1, 2026, 7:42 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MOGADISHU, Somalia -- MOGADISHU, Somalia (AP) — Somali pirates have seized an Iranian fishing vessel carrying 23 people, the Maritime Security Center Indian Ocean said, warning that the ship was approaching a commercial shipping lane and could become a floating base for further attacks.
The Azini was hijacked Thursday between the coastal towns of Bandar Bayla and Hafun in northeastern Somalia, a maritime security officer with the Puntland Maritime Police Force said Sunday.
The officer told The Associated Press that 12 pirates seized the vessel, which was carrying 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak with the media.
The crew’s safety was unknown, the center said in an alert dated Saturday. In an updated warning, it said that pirates could use the vessel as a “mother ship” to support attacks on commercial vessels.
The European Union’s naval Operation Atalanta was investigating. The center urged ships in the area to remain vigilant and report suspicious activity.
The seizure follows a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, with some attacks taking place far from Somalia’s coastline. The captures included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
